`whodunit investigate cases/whole-history.toml --from-traffic refund-agent --fresh`, with everything from stage 2 in it. It took 10 minutes 46 seconds and 176 replays, about 80 cents. I had said 50 to 60 cents beforehand, and the difference is the second patch.

- The lineup named the same commit, `ced2ecd`, at 98.3% after 20 replays across 5 commits. Sunday's run had 99.8%. This time one of the 8 replays from the culprit on passed.
- No replay was voided and none timed out.
- The request was checked against the transcript, and `entire why` put all 4 changed lines behind the same commit, checkpoint and request.
- The brief gives the rate as 75%, 11 of 14 runs, and says the evidence does not show why some runs pass. I read it against the record before quoting it anywhere.
- The first patch went 30 replays without a failure on its own case. Under Sunday morning's code it would have been kept. The do-no-harm check replayed 13 other requests on it, and "Please refund order 1001 for customer cust_9." went wrong in 8 of 8 replays, against 5 of 8 before the patch. So the patch was not kept. The second patch was told what the first had done, went 30 replays without a failure, and made none of the 13 worse. It is the kept fix.
- The investigation is trace `b842b67dfae39c67c1a3aa76772f5229` in neatlogs cloud.
- The record has its rounds, so the page's "Replay the investigation" plays the real ones. It was watched in a browser on another case from start to the ring.

Three things to be straight about.

The rejection was a near thing. That ordinary refund was already failing 5 times in 8 before the patch, because the branch a fix starts from still carries the other four regressions. 8 of 8 against 5 of 8 comes to a 4.4% chance that the patch made nothing worse, just under the 5% line. The page first said the patch "broke a request that had been going right", which the numbers beside it contradicted. It now says the patch made the request go wrong more often than before, and so do the README, the script and the post draft, which I had written the wrong way a few minutes earlier.

The cost line was wrong again, for a new reason. Yesterday's fix billed a case for replays between its first and its last. With the harm checks added on Sunday evening, that stretch now covered Sunday afternoon's plain-bisect experiment, and four cases were billed for it. Each step that replays now records its own stretch of time, and a case is billed for those stretches only. The six cases come to 1,380 replays and about $7.01. `pitch/business-plan.md` has the new table. Its runway table was not worked out again, and says by how much it is off.

The ablation is real now. Run without alibis and without ordinary runs, the same case took 33 replays across 8 commits to reach 99.0% on the same commit, against 20 across 5. Sunday's pair was 30 against 20. `cases/whole-history.ablation.json` is written by the run and no longer entered by hand.

Also in this commit:

- Every page was checked by script at 1280 px and at a true 375 px, in a frame, because Chrome will not make a window that narrow. Two things spilled and are fixed: a margin note with a long unbroken string, and the suspects table on a phone, which now stacks. Nothing scrolls sideways except the lineup.
- `evidence/` has new screenshots, all on light paper: the headline page whole, its top with the lineup, its Fix section, the same page at phone width, the case closed by a revert, the open case, and the docket. The two screenshots of the first planted cases are removed. Their records stay. They were accepted on 8 and 6 clean replays under the first standard, and drawing them with the new page would have stamped them closed, which today's bar would not.
- `cases/og.png` is the picture a link preview shows, drawn from `cases/og.html`. A page points at it by a relative path until `WHODUNIT_SITE` gives the casebook's public address.
- `eval/simulator/README.md` has the two-culprit table.

Not done, and the noon cutoff is near: the two-change-point model is still not in the lineup, the casebook has no public address, and the forwarding of each case's two runs to neatlogs cloud still waits on `neatroots cloud login`.

### 11:41 AM, Monday: last things before the cutoff

- The lineup had made every suspect a tab stop, 58 of them on the headline page, ahead of everything else. A column is no longer one. The lineup's scroll box takes focus, and the table under it holds each column's details.
- `AGENTS.md` says where things stand as of Monday noon, and what is left over from the review: the two-change-point model is not wired in, and two things wait on the owner, `neatroots cloud login` and the dashboard's address for a trace.
- Gateway spend for this session, by estimate: about 50 cents of larger-model calls for briefs and patches, and about $1.40 of replays for the four harm checks, the headline rerun and the ablation. That puts the gateway at about $16 of $20.

Nothing was pushed, posted, written to cfo.ai or launched on AWS in this job. After this entry, fixes only.

### 12:22 PM, Monday: the case file redone in an indie app design system

The owner asked for this after the noon cutoff, so it is new work at the owner's request. The ask was to redesign the pages with a design system made for small indie apps, to pick what applies, and to say what was left out. Only the look changed. The records, the wording of each section and every number are what they were this morning.

What was chosen:

- Mood cream with one accent, terracotta. The system's default is a cooler grey with amber. Cream was picked because the old paper was warm and the red ring on the culprit carries over as terracotta ink.
- The system's stylesheet is in `whodunit/casefile/foundation.css`, as given and unedited. `casefile.css` is now only what the page adds, and takes every colour, radius and shadow from the foundation's tokens. The one exception is the terminal window's four text colours, which stay fixed in both papers the way a window's traffic lights do.
- Kept from the system: the floating pill nav with section anchors, a status badge, pill buttons, cards with a hairline ring, a soft stage under the lineup, mono for SHAs and counts, and on the casebook a dark terminal window on the warm wallpaper.
- Left out: the faux menu bar, the popover and the phone frame, because Whodunit is a command and a page. The blur on the nav, because `AGENTS.md` rules glass out, so the pill is solid. Icon tiles, the three-card grid, pricing, FAQ, social proof and scroll reveals, because a case page has nothing to sell.
- Changed in kind: the rotated rubber stamp is a status badge, filled only for a closed case. The typed form is a facts card. Disclosures are pills with a plus that turns to a cross.
- The lineup keeps its own drawing, with the typed marks, the strike-through, the hatching and the pencil ring.
- A case page's headline is now the question, "57 commits since it last worked. Which one did it?", and the report sits under it. The casebook's headline is "Which commit did it, and why."
- The terminal on the casebook is made from the headline case's record with the same sentences `whodunit investigate` prints. I checked each line against `whodunit/cli.py` and the numbers against the record.

What went wrong on the way:

- The first casebook lead said Whodunit replays requests "against every suspect commit". The headline case tested 5 of 57. It now says the replays go on until one commit stands out.
- The 57-suspect lineup is 1,122 px wide and the card it sat in was 1,024, so the first four suspects were cut off. The lineup's stage is now let out to 1,240 px, past the text column.
- With the symptom as the headline, the headline case ran to five lines at display size. That is what led to the question as headline.
- I gave the Log two-column rows and the rule also caught the list of tries in the Fix section. Every run of text there became its own 86 px column and the section went from 630 px tall to 2,246. It showed up as a page height that made no sense when I measured for the screenshots. The rule now applies to the Log alone.
- The two buttons the script adds carry `hidden`, and a pill sets its own display, so with scripting off they would have shown and done nothing. A rule now makes the attribute win, and a test checks it is on the page.
- The screenshot script stops as soon as its target file has something in it. The first retake of `cases/og.png` therefore left the old picture in place and reported success. I saw it only because I opened the file. Shots now go to an empty folder and are copied over.
- The foundation has a comment that mentions following the system's dark setting, and a test checks that the page never does by searching for that phrase. Pages now carry both stylesheets without comments. The files keep theirs.

What was checked:

- 150 fast tests pass. The page tests were rewritten for the new markup and gained four checks: the closed badge, the mood and accent on the page, no blur on the nav, and the terminal made from a record.
- All seven pages at 1440 px and at a true 375 px: nothing is wider than the frame except the lineup's own scroll box.
- "Replay the investigation" was pressed in a headless browser on `cents-off`: seven rounds, ending on all 21 marks and "Replay again". The paper toggle set the dark tokens and relabelled itself "Light".
- Dark paper was looked at on the casebook and the headline case. Both empty states were looked at, and lost links that pointed at a lineup that was not there.
- The system's own checklist: one mood and one accent, every control a pill, headlines in sentence case of three lines or fewer, body text under 680 px, small text no fainter than the third ink, focus rings, reduced motion.

Not checked: a real phone, any browser other than Chrome, and the page with the web fonts blocked.

`evidence/` has all seven screenshots retaken, and `cases/og.png` is redrawn from `cases/og.html` in the new look. `AGENTS.md` has the new design section in place of the typed paper one. Nothing was pushed.

### 1:15 PM, Monday: the business plan is in cfo.ai

The owner signed in to the cfo.ai server and said yes to the whole build after seeing the list of writes and the numbers they would produce. The workspace was empty before.

What is in it:

- Six pages: Whodunit plan, Assumptions, Customers and revenue, Costs and margin, Cash and runway, Simulator. Each opens with a short note on where its numbers come from. The first page says that no real customer has used the refund agent and that its traffic was sent by a script.
- Eight tables. Four hold inputs: the six measured investigations, unit costs, pricing and customers, fixed costs and cash. Three are monthly, October 2026 to September 2027, and every line in them is a formula on those inputs. The eighth puts cash in the four cases side by side.
- Four scenarios: Base, Downside, Downside with no founder draw, and Upside. They differ in five inputs: the two Team targets, the Scale target, churn and the draw.
- Three live blocks: the year at a glance, cash by case, and a simulator with sliders for the Team price, usage, the cost of an investigation and the founder draw.

The cost of an investigation is not typed in. The model takes the mean of the six measured replay costs, $1.17, and adds $0.20 for the brief and the patch.

How it was checked. I worked the twelve months out by hand in a script first, for all four cases, then ran the tables as a dry run that saves nothing, then wrote them. The saved model gives the script's numbers to the cent: $23,141 after month 12 in the base case, minus $5,300 in the downside, $12,700 in the downside with no draw, and $70,178 in the upside. All three blocks render without errors in cfo.ai's own check, in both themes.

What changed against `pitch/business-plan.md`, which is now rewritten to match:

- The old runway table charged every paying agent $26 a month to serve. A Scale agent runs 125 investigations a month at half use and has a worker of its own, which comes to about $232. With that, base cash after month 12 is $23,141 where the old table said $26,113, and the upside is $70,178 where it said $76,750.
- The downside with the draw runs out in month 10. The old table said month 11.
- I tried to reproduce the old table before replacing it. The downside rows came out exactly and the base and upside rows did not, by $244 and $976, and I could not find what the old sums had done differently.
- The conclusion is the same: the plan survives the downside only if the founder takes no draw.

What went wrong on the way:

- The simulator first showed $23,134 for the saved plan, $7 off, because I had rounded the cost of an investigation to the cent before using it. It now uses the model's own value and shows $23,141.
- One of its four headline numbers was cut off at "Not this ye". The numbers now sit two to a row.
- The overview page first got a cocktail glass for an icon, which is what cfo.ai matched to "magnifying glass". It is a search icon now.

Not done, or not checked:

- Clicks. cfo.ai's check renders a block and does not move a slider, so the sliders have been read as code and never dragged.
- The model leaves out replays billed at cost plus 20% for customers on a large model, and extra investigations at $8.
- Churn only sets how many agents have to be signed each month. The targets do not fall with it.
- The workspace is private. A share link for the judges is an outward step and is the owner's to make.

`evidence/` has two renders from cfo.ai, the cash chart and the simulator. Nothing was pushed.

### 1:30 PM, Monday: the repo is public, and three more pieces of evidence

The owner said yes to the first push after seeing what it would publish. Before asking, I counted what the recorded sessions hold, without printing any of it. No key-shaped strings and no email addresses. The owner's home folder path is in 242 files, two account ids in 114, the file names of the owner's private notes in 163, the names of other connectors in 162, and the cfo.ai workspace name in 6. `.env` was never committed.

- The repo is at https://github.com/kinnuworks/whodunit, with `main` and `entire/checkpoints/v1`. Entire's own hook pushed the checkpoints while `main` went up, so my separate push of that branch was refused as already there. Both branches match the local ones. The six fix branches were not pushed.
- The Entire page for the culprit's checkpoint does not open yet. It answers 404 signed out and signed in, because Entire has no repository for this account. Its start page offers to mirror a GitHub repository, which asks for access to the owner's GitHub account, so that step is left for the owner. Until then the public proof is the commit on GitHub with its `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and the checkpoints branch.
- Three screenshots from the neatlogs dashboard are in `evidence/`, taken in the owner's browser with the owner's name and photo cut off: the traces list, the investigation's own trace with its 17 steps, and a scripted refund run with four tool errors flagged. I left out the detection's trend chart because it drew empty at every range I tried.
- The cfo.ai plan has a read-only link the owner asked for, in `evidence/README.md`.

### 2:06 PM, Monday: the casebook is live, the checkpoint page opens, and there is a video

- The owner mirrored the repo into Entire, and the checkpoint page for the headline culprit now opens without an account. Every case page links its culprit to its own Entire page, and all four distinct links answer.
- The casebook is published from `cases/` to https://kinnuworks.github.io/whodunit/ by a small workflow, with the owner's yes.
- The owner asked for the demo video to be made as a motion film. It is 89 seconds, ten scenes, captions and a score with no voice. `pitch/video/` has the film's scenes, the redrawn screens, the data and a contact sheet, and says what is real and what is drawn. The lineup scene plays the headline record's own four rounds.

It took two rounds of stills. The first had every panel too small in the frame, the git log scrolling over its own title bar, an empty frame at five of the cuts, and the request in the Entire scene still being typed when its panel left. The caption check also caught four captions on screen for less time than it takes to read them.

Not checked: nobody has watched it at full speed with sound. I looked at stills and at four frames pulled from the finished file. There is no 9 by 16 cut.

### 2:21 PM, Monday: the video gets a voice

The owner asked for a narrated cut with a title card. The narration is a synthesized voice from ElevenLabs, on the owner's account, about 1,600 characters of the month's allowance. The first thirteen calls failed before anything was sent, because the folders they were told to write to did not exist.

The film is now 2 minutes 16 seconds and thirteen scenes. Three are new: a title card, before and after the fix (11 of 14 runs wrong, then 0 of 30), and one card each for what neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai do in the product. Every scene is as long as its narration clip, and the script that builds the film works out where each phrase falls so the picture changes on the word.

The clips are played 6% faster than they were made. At their own speed the film came to 144 seconds, and a post on X can carry 140.

The voice sits about 12 dB over the music while it speaks, measured on the two stems. The finished file is at about minus 15 LUFS.

Not checked: I cannot listen to it. I measured levels and where each clip starts and ends, and looked at stills. Whether the voice says "neatlogs" and "cfo.ai" the way a person would is for the owner's ears.

### 6:00 PM, a case from one trace

Stage 2, fourth item. Until now a case file was written by hand: someone had to know the failing input, what it should have produced, and both ends of the range. `whodunit open-case --from-trace <id>` writes the file from one failing run and stops.

- It looks for the run in neatroots, and in neatlogs cloud if neatroots does not have it.
- The input is the root span's. The bad ref is the commit in the run_info tags.
- The expected result is what the nearest earlier run of the same input paid, among runs that passed. A run passed if it was not flagged and paid something different from the failing run.
- The good ref comes from `whodunit/onset.py`: every run of that input, judged against the expected result, goes through the same change-point model the lineup uses, and the range starts where that model is 99% sure nothing had gone wrong yet.
- If no earlier run passed, it asks one question: what should this request have produced? Away from a keyboard it prints the question, writes nothing and exits, and `--expect` gives the answer.
- A trace does not say how to build and run the agent, so that is copied from another case for the same agent.

Tried on the real traces, on an ordinary run from the traffic that refunded 30.00 on someone else's order. From the trace id alone it wrote a case with the right request, an expected result of no refund taken from a run 11 hours of traffic earlier, and a range of 41 suspects that holds the real culprit. That file went to a scratch folder and is not in `cases/`.

What it cannot do: the earlier runs of the same input are read from neatroots only. A trace that exists only in the cloud gets its input and its bad ref, and then has to be told the expected result and the good ref. And "passed" leans on neatroots' own flags, so a run that was wrong without being flagged, and wrong in a different way from the failing one, could be taken for the expected result. The file's first lines name the run the expectation came from, so a person can check it.

### 6:21 PM, when no commit did it
# Sealed eval, 11 October 2026

Five regressions were planted in the refund agent's history by a second coding session, through ordinary requests to fresh coding sessions. It wrote the answer key, and the key's SHA-256 was committed in 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case. `eval/score.py` checks the key against that hash before scoring. The key was added to git only after every case had been run.

Replays ran on the hackathon gateway's small model, three at a time.

## Result

With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 cases where nobody was named.

The two open cases were then resumed from their own replays with up to 200 more allowed: 5 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations.

| Case | Rate the second session measured | Rate Whodunit estimated | At 120 replays | In the end | Replays | Commits replayed | Suspects |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| cents-off | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 21 | 5 | 13 |
| wrong-order-refunded | 30% | 12% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 9 | 12 |
| half-done-batch | 25% | 14% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 10 | 15 |
| strangers-paid | 72% | 59% | solved | solved | 30 | 5 | 11 |
| turned-away | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 24 | 6 | 14 |

The rate Whodunit estimates is a posterior mean, so after only a few replays it sits below 100% even for a bug that fails every time.

## What it cost

Replay spend on the gateway, estimated from token counts at list prices, came to about $1.91 for all five cases:

- cents-off: about $0.08 (61,267 tokens)
- wrong-order-refunded: about $0.57 (438,034 tokens)
- half-done-batch: about $1.04 (795,110 tokens)
- strangers-paid: about $0.10 (78,530 tokens)
- turned-away: about $0.12 (100,111 tokens)

## What this does and does not show

- No commit was wrongly accused, at either budget. Five cases cannot show how often that would hold. The simulator puts a number on it for cases shaped like the two rare ones: with 320 replays allowed, about 4% of accusations name the wrong commit, and with 120 about 13%. See `eval/simulator/README.md`. On `half-done-batch` the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody. That is the behaviour the 95% bar is for.
- The two cases it could not close at 120 replays are the two that fail least often. Whodunit put them at 12% and 14%, where the second session had measured 30% and 25% from a handful of probes. A bug that rare needs a lot of replays whatever the method.
- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects. On ranges this size a careful scan from the oldest commit would have replayed about as many commits as Whodunit did, so this eval says little about savings on long histories. The simulator in `eval/simulator` covers 40 suspects.
- Five cases is a small sample. It is enough to say the pipeline works on a history it did not write, and not enough to put a number on accuracy.
- Each case has one planted regression inside its range, by design. Two regressions that touch the same inputs in one range are outside what the model assumes.

## What happened after the culprits were named

The owner's ruling was patch for all three kinds of change involved. A fix is kept when its failure rate is 95% likely to be back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit. The last column gives what the replays of the kept fix showed and the 95% upper bound on its failure rate. Clearing the bar is not proof: in simulation a fix that still fails 4 runs in 100 clears it about one time in three.

| Case | Outcome | Tries | Replays of the final fix, and the most it could still fail at 95% |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| cents-off | patch kept | 1 | 0 failures in 30, at most 6.2% |
| strangers-paid | patch kept | 1 | 0 failures in 30, at most 6.2% |
| wrong-order-refunded | patch kept | 1 | 0 failures in 36, at most 5.2% |
| turned-away | two patches fell short, then a revert was kept | 3 | 0 failures in 30, at most 6.2% |
| half-done-batch | not fixed | 3 | two patches left 5 failures in 90 each, at most 10.6%, and the revert conflicts |

So four of five were closed, one of them only by giving up on the patch the owner asked for, and one was left open and says so.

## The same culprit across the whole history

`cases/whole-history.toml` takes the `strangers-paid` regression and widens the range to the whole grown history, 57 suspects. With alibis from entire-graph for 22 of them and 18 ordinary runs as evidence, 20 replays across 5 commits named the culprit at 99.8%. A scan from the oldest suspect would have tested 37 commits. This is the run that speaks to savings on a longer history, and it is one run. Run again with no alibis and no ordinary runs to go on, it took 30 replays across 8 commits to reach 95.4%. So the head start saved 10 replays and 3 commits, in one run each way, with the two kinds of help taken away together.

Both runs were made again on Monday 12 October, from nothing. With the head start: 20 replays across 5 commits, 98.3%. Without it: 33 replays across 8 commits, 99.0%. That run also went on to the fix, and its first patch was rejected by the do-no-harm check. `cases/whole-history.casefile.html` has it.

I'm drafting the top of the README now, introducing Whodunit with a punchy tagline and starting a table that highlights the "one case, one command" value proposition.

Finishing the table with rows for what went wrong, which commit caused it, who requested it, what it cost, and how it was fixed, then adding a note that `git bisect` can't catch intermittent failures like this. I'm also drafting a disclosure paragraph clarifying what's real versus staged in the demo, explaining that the refund agent's commits came from real coding-agent sessions but one regression was deliberately planted among them.

I need to correct myself on the commit count -- the actual source says 55 commits via eval/ask.sh growing to 57, not that each of 57 was session-generated, so I should soften that claim.

Now I'm adding a linked screenshot of the case lineup pointing to the live case page, noting the project was built for neatHack between October 10-12, 2026, with hackathon.md as the honest build log. I'm also describing the single command that runs an investigation end-to-end, stopping only to ask the user one clarifying question.

Each step in the pipeline maps to a recorded case file: opening a case from a trace id (which happened off the record, in a scratch folder, documented only in the build log), narrowing the suspect lineup from 57 down through alibi checks and replay testing to pinpoint one commit at 98.3% confidence, and then establishing the motive by matching the request against a specific checkpoint and tracing all four changed lines back to that same commit.

From there, the brief cites six sentences each tied to a span, commit, or checkpoint, and the ruling for revert-versus-patch follows a precedent set by the owner on a prior case so it doesn't need to ask again. Patches get tested through replay batches checking both effectiveness and harm to unrelated requests — one patch gets thrown out after breaking other refunds, a second one gets kept after clearing the harm threshold, another case reverts after repeated patch failures, and one case stays open entirely when neither patching nor reverting clears the bar.

Now I'm tallying the damage from the whole-history case — four of six ordinary runs went wrong, totaling $120 paid out across 176 replays at about 80 cents apiece — and building the evidence table linking each claim back to its source: the fix section of the headline case, the replay statistics, and the neatlogs trace screenshot showing the investigation itself as a trace.

I'm compiling a table pointing to the underlying evidence: entire.io checkpoints behind the culprit commit, the cfo.ai financial plan, the failed-then-corrected action log, public posts from the hackathon, and the dated commit history. I'm also double-checking whether the Fix section actually includes the "before" numbers I claimed.

The casefile's whole-page history shows 11 of 14 failures before the fix and 0 failures in 30 after, so I'll link to that screenshot rather than just the fix anchor. The other sections — "Why plain bisect is not enough," "How a case runs," and the refund agent history paragraph — can stay mostly as-is, so I'm focusing on replacing just the opening lines of the README with this corrected framing.

from __future__ import annotations

import os
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Protocol

DEFAULT_MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5"  # the support agent is PINNED to Haiku tier; see evals/models.py


@dataclass
class Response:
    """Normalized model response. `content` is a list of Anthropic-style blocks:
    {"type": "text", "text": ...} or {"type": "tool_use", "id": ..., "name": ..., "input": {...}}."""

    content: list[dict[str, Any]]
    stop_reason: str = "end_turn"
    input_tokens: int = 0
    output_tokens: int = 0

    @property
    def text(self) -> str:
        return "".join(b["text"] for b in self.content if b["type"] == "text")

    @property
    def tool_uses(self) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        return [b for b in self.content if b["type"] == "tool_use"]


class Provider(Protocol):
    def create(self, *, system: str, messages: list[dict[str, Any]], tools: list[dict[str, Any]],
               max_tokens: int = 1024) -> Response: ...

    """Anthropic Messages API. Key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, model from AGENT_MODEL, temperature 0."""

            from anthropic import Anthropic

            from agent.tracing import wrap_client

            model=self.model, max_tokens=max_tokens,
            extra_body={"temperature": 0},  # SDK 1.x dropped the typed kwarg; the API still accepts it
            system=system, messages=messages, tools=tools,
        )
        blocks: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
        for b in r.content:
            if b.type == "text":
                blocks.append({"type": "text", "text": b.text})
            elif b.type == "tool_use":
                blocks.append({"type": "tool_use", "id": b.id, "name": b.name, "input": dict(b.input)})

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import time
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from typing import Any

from agent.logs import log_message_truncated, log_tool_call
from agent.prompt import SYSTEM_PROMPT
from agent.provider import Provider
from agent.tracing import current_trace_id, set_json, span, traced
from tools import ToolBox

MAX_STEPS = 12  # model calls per run; leaves room for verification searches and retries
MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS = 2000  # longer customer messages are truncated (and the truncation logged)
_UNKNOWN_ORDER = re.compile(r"^order '(.*)' not found$")


def unknown_order_reply(order_id: str) -> str:
    return (f"Sorry, I couldn't find an order with the number {order_id}. Could you double-check the order "
            "number and send it again? Is there anything else we can help with?")


def _guard_unknown_order(reply: str, tool_calls: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> str:
    """Replace a reply that echoes a raw 'order ... not found' tool error with a customer-friendly apology."""
    for tc in tool_calls:
        err = tc["result"].get("error", "")
        m = _UNKNOWN_ORDER.match(err)
        if m and err.lower() in reply.lower():
            return unknown_order_reply(m.group(1))
    return reply


@dataclass
class RunResult:
    reply: str
    tool_calls: list[dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=list)  # {name, args, result}
    steps: int = 0
    input_tokens: int = 0
    output_tokens: int = 0
    trace_id: str = ""
    hit_step_limit: bool = False

    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return asdict(self)


def run_agent(message: str, provider: Provider, toolbox: ToolBox | None = None,
              max_steps: int | None = None) -> RunResult:
    """Run one customer message through the agent. `max_steps` defaults to MAX_STEPS.
    Messages longer than MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS are truncated to that length."""
    if len(message) > MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS:
        log_message_truncated(len(message), MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS)
        message = message[:MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS]
    return _run(message, provider, toolbox or ToolBox(), max_steps or MAX_STEPS)


@traced
def _run(message: str, provider: Provider, toolbox: ToolBox, max_steps: int) -> RunResult:
    res = RunResult(reply="", trace_id=current_trace_id())
    messages: list[dict[str, Any]] = [{"role": "user", "content": message}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        r = provider.create(system=SYSTEM_PROMPT, messages=messages, tools=toolbox.schemas)
        res.steps += 1
        res.input_tokens += r.input_tokens
        res.output_tokens += r.output_tokens
        if not r.tool_uses:
            res.reply = _guard_unknown_order(r.text, res.tool_calls)
            return res
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
        results = []
        for tu in r.tool_uses:
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            with span(f"tool:{tu['name']}", "TOOL", **{"tool.name": tu["name"]}) as sp:
                set_json(sp, "tool.args", tu["input"])
                out = toolbox.call(tu["name"], tu["input"])
                set_json(sp, "tool.result", out)
                if isinstance(out, dict) and "error" in out:
                    sp.set_attribute("tool.error", str(out["error"])[:500])
            log_tool_call(tu["name"], tu["input"], (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
            res.tool_calls.append({"name": tu["name"], "args": tu["input"], "result": out})
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": tu["id"], "content": json.dumps(out)})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
        res.reply = r.text
    res.hit_step_limit = True
    if not res.reply:
        res.reply = "Sorry, I could not finish handling this request. A human agent will follow up."
    return res

"""Replay a case's inputs against a commit, in a git worktree of its own."""

import hashlib
import os
import signal
import subprocess
import threading
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

from .case import Case, CaseInput, judge, last_json_line
from .neat import unnamed
from .suspects import git, resolve

PASS, FAIL, SKIP = "pass", "fail", "skip"
VOID = "void"  # the provider or the network failed every time it was tried, so the replay says nothing about the commit
VOID_WAITS = (2.0, 8.0)  # seconds to wait before the second and the third attempt after a provider error


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Replay:
    sha: str
    input: str
    verdict: str  # pass, fail, skip or void
    reason: str
    seconds: float
    started: float = 0.0  # wall clock, seconds since the epoch
    tag: str = ""  # the case tag this replay's run carries in its trace, unique to the replay
    voided: int = 0  # attempts that hit a provider or network error and were thrown away
    timeouts: int = 0  # attempts that ran out of time
    model: str = ""  # a fingerprint of the model id the agent reported, if it reported one. Not the id itself.
    lock: str = ""  # the first 12 characters of the hash of the lockfile it ran with


def run_command(command: list[str], cwd: Path, env: dict, timeout: float) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    """Like subprocess.run, but a timeout stops the whole process group.

    The replay command is usually `uv run ...`, which starts the agent as a child. Killing only
    `uv` would leave the agent running.
    """
    process = subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=cwd, env=env, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, start_new_session=True)
    try:
        stdout, stderr = process.communicate(timeout=timeout)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        try:
            os.killpg(process.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
        except ProcessLookupError:
            pass
        process.communicate()
        raise
    return subprocess.CompletedProcess(command, process.returncode, stdout, stderr)


class Runner:
    """Keeps one worktree per commit under .whodunit/worktrees and counts every replay it runs."""

    def __init__(self, repo: str | Path, case: Case, keep: bool = False):
        self.repo = Path(repo).resolve()
        self.case = case
        self.keep = keep
        # One folder per runner, so two runs in the same repo never remove each other's worktrees.
        self.root = self.repo / ".whodunit" / "worktrees" / str(os.getpid())
        self.built: dict[str, str | None] = {}  # sha -> None if the build worked, else why it did not
        self.replays: list[Replay] = []
        self._locks: dict[str, threading.Lock] = defaultdict(threading.Lock)  # one build at a time per commit
        self._turn: dict[str, int] = defaultdict(int)  # which input a commit gets next
        self._count = 0
        self._first = int(time.time()) % 100000 * 1000  # so tags from separate runs of one case never collide
        self.void_waits: tuple[float, ...] = VOID_WAITS
        subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(self.repo), "worktree", "prune"], capture_output=True)

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        if not self.keep:
            self.clean()

    def worktree(self, sha: str) -> Path:
        path = self.root / sha[:12]
        if not path.exists():
            self.root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            git(self.repo, "worktree", "add", "--detach", "--force", str(path), sha)
        return path

    def clean(self) -> None:
        for sha in list(self.built):
            path = self.root / sha[:12]
            if path.exists():
                subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(self.repo), "worktree", "remove", "--force", str(path)], capture_output=True)
        self.built.clear()
        try:
            self.root.rmdir()
        except OSError:
            pass

    def _lock(self, sha: str) -> str:
        """The hash of the agent's lockfile at this commit, or nothing if it has none."""
        lock = self.root / sha[:12] / self.case.target / "uv.lock"

def run_command(command: list[str], cwd: Path, env: dict, timeout: float) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    """Like subprocess.run, but a timeout stops the whole process group.

    The replay command is usually `uv run ...`, which starts the agent as a child. Killing only
    `uv` would leave the agent running.
    """
    process = subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=cwd, env=env, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, start_new_session=True)
    try:
        stdout, stderr = process.communicate(timeout=timeout)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        try:
            os.killpg(process.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
        except ProcessLookupError:
            pass

"""The suspects: every commit after the last good ref, up to and including the first bad one."""

import subprocess
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

# A commit that never touched the agent's folder can still be guilty (a shared file, a
# lockfile higher up), so it keeps a small prior. Plain bisect ignores priors.
PRIOR_TOUCHES_TARGET = 1.0
PRIOR_ELSEWHERE = 0.05


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Suspect:
    sha: str
    subject: str
    files: tuple[str, ...]
    checkpoint: str | None  # Entire checkpoint id from the commit trailer
    touches_target: bool
    prior: float
    alibi: str = ""  # why this commit starts with less suspicion, when entire-graph gives a reason

    @property
    def short(self) -> str:
        return self.sha[:12]


def git(repo: str | Path, *args: str) -> str:
    done = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(repo), *args], capture_output=True, text=True)
    if done.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f"git {' '.join(args)} failed: {done.stderr.strip()}")
    return done.stdout


def resolve(repo: str | Path, ref: str) -> str:
    return git(repo, "rev-parse", "--verify", f"{ref}^{{commit}}").strip()


def list_suspects(repo: str | Path, good: str, bad: str, target: str = ".", graph: bool = False) -> list[Suspect]:
    """Commits in good..bad, oldest first. The last one is the bad ref itself.

    The path filter gives the first prior: a commit that never touched the agent's folder keeps
    a small one. With `graph`, entire-graph refines it for the commits that did, by asking
    whether what they changed is something the agent runs.
    """
    shas = git(repo, "rev-list", "--reverse", "--ancestry-path", f"{good}..{bad}").split()
    prefix = "" if target in (".", "") else target.rstrip("/") + "/"
    suspects = []
    for sha in shas:
        subject, _, trailer = git(
            repo, "show", "-s", "--format=%s%x00%(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly,separator=%x20)", sha
        ).strip().partition("\x00")
        files = tuple(git(repo, "diff-tree", "--no-commit-id", "--name-only", "-r", "-m", "--first-parent", sha).split("\n"))
        files = tuple(f for f in files if f)
        touches = any(f.startswith(prefix) for f in files)
        prior, alibi = (PRIOR_TOUCHES_TARGET, "") if touches else (PRIOR_ELSEWHERE, "never touched the agent's folder")
        if graph and touches:
            from .graph import alibi as graph_alibi  # imported here because graph.py uses git() from this module

            prior, reason = graph_alibi(repo, sha, target)
            alibi = reason if prior < 1.0 else ""
        suspects.append(Suspect(
            sha=sha, subject=subject, files=files, checkpoint=trailer.split()[0] if trailer.strip() else None,
            touches_target=touches, prior=prior, alibi=alibi,
        ))
    return suspects

"""The suspects: every commit after the last good ref, up to and including the first bad one."""

import subprocess
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

# A commit that never touched the agent's folder can still be guilty (a shared file, a
# lockfile higher up), so it keeps a small prior. Plain bisect ignores priors.
PRIOR_TOUCHES_TARGET = 1.0
PRIOR_ELSEWHERE = 0.05


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Suspect:
    sha: str
    subject: str
    files: tuple[str, ...]
    checkpoint: str | None  # Entire checkpoint id from the commit trailer
    touches_target: bool
    prior: float
    alibi: str = ""  # why this commit starts with less suspicion, when entire-graph gives a reason

    @property
    def short(self) -> str:
        return self.sha[:12]


def git(repo: str | Path, *args: str) -> str:
    done = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(repo), *args], capture_output=True, text=True)
    if done.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f"git {' '.join(args)} failed: {done.stderr.strip()}")
    return done.stdout


def resolve(repo: str | Path, ref: str) -> str:
    return git(repo, "rev-parse", "--verify", f"{ref}^{{commit}}").strip()


def list_suspects(repo: str | Path, good: str, bad: str, target: str = ".", graph: bool = False) -> list[Suspect]:
    """Commits in good..bad, oldest first. The last one is the bad ref itself.

    The path filter gives the first prior: a commit that never touched the agent's folder keeps
    a small one. With `graph`, entire-graph refines it for the commits that did, by asking
    whether what they changed is something the agent runs.
    """
    shas = git(repo, "rev-list", "--reverse", "--ancestry-path", f"{good}..{bad}").split()
    prefix = "" if target in (".", "") else target.rstrip("/") + "/"
    suspects = []
    for sha in shas:
        subject, _, trailer = git(
            repo, "show", "-s", "--format=%s%x00%(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly,separator=%x20)", sha
        ).strip().partition("\x00")
        files = tuple(git(repo, "diff-tree", "--no-commit-id", "--name-only", "-r", "-m", "--first-parent", sha).split("\n"))
        files = tuple(f for f in files if f)
        touches = any(f.startswith(prefix) for f in files)
        prior, alibi = (PRIOR_TOUCHES_TARGET, "") if touches else (PRIOR_ELSEWHERE, "never touched the agent's folder")
        if graph and touches:
            from .graph import alibi as graph_alibi  # imported here because graph.py uses git() from this module

            prior, reason = graph_alibi(repo, sha, target)
            alibi = reason if prior < 1.0 else ""
        suspects.append(Suspect(
            sha=sha, subject=subject, files=files, checkpoint=trailer.split()[0] if trailer.strip() else None,
            touches_target=touches, prior=prior, alibi=alibi,
        ))
    return suspects

    with a brace at the start of a line and runs to the end.
    """
    text = stdout.strip()

            except json.JSONDecodeError:

            if isinstance(block, dict):

    return None


def _at(result: dict, path: str):
    """A value inside the printed result, by a dotted path such as "output.tool_calls"."""
    for key in path.split("."):
        if not isinstance(result, dict) or key not in result:
            return None
        result = result[key]
    return result


def _fits(got, want) -> bool:
    """Whether an argument has the wanted value.

    A plain value has to be equal, with numbers compared to half a cent and strings without
    their outer spaces. A table asks for something looser and holds exactly one of: `in` (any
    of these), `contains` and `regex` (both ignoring case), `gte` and `lte`.
    """
    if isinstance(want, dict):
        if len(want) != 1:
            raise ValueError(f"an argument matcher holds one of in, contains, regex, gte, lte, and this one holds {sorted(want)}")
        (how, value), = want.items()
        if how == "in":
            return any(_fits(got, one) for one in value)
        if how == "contains":
            return got is not None and str(value).lower() in str(got).lower()
        if how == "regex":
            return got is not None and re.search(value, str(got), re.IGNORECASE) is not None
        if how in ("gte", "lte"):
            number = isinstance(got, (int, float)) and not isinstance(got, bool)
            return number and (got >= value if how == "gte" else got <= value)
        raise ValueError(f"argument matcher {how!r} is not one of in, contains, regex, gte, lte")
    if isinstance(want, (int, float)) and not isinstance(want, bool):
        return isinstance(got, (int, float)) and not isinstance(got, bool) and math.isclose(got, want, abs_tol=0.005)
    if isinstance(want, str) and isinstance(got, str):
        return got.strip() == want.strip()
    return got == want

def _calls_verdict(check: dict, expect: dict, result: dict) -> tuple[bool, str]:

    unknown = sorted(set(expect) - set(CALLS_EXPECT))
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"a calls check does not know {unknown}. It knows {', '.join(CALLS_EXPECT)}.")
    name_key, args_key = check.get("name", "name"), check.get("args", "args")
    calls = _at(result, check.get("calls", "tool_calls"))
    calls = [c for c in calls if isinstance(c, dict)] if isinstance(calls, list) else []
    names = [str(c.get(name_key)) for c in calls]
    reply = _at(result, check.get("reply", "reply"))
    reply = reply if isinstance(reply, str) else ""
    said = f"called {', '.join(names) or 'nothing'}"

    if missing:
        return False, f"never called {', '.join(missing)} ({said})"
    made = [tool for tool in expect.get("must_not_call", []) if tool in names]
    if made:
        return False, f"called {', '.join(made)}, which it should not have"
    first = expect.get("first_call")
    if first and names[:1] != [first]:
        return False, f"the first call was {names[0] if names else 'none'}, expected {first}"
    for tool, times in (expect.get("call_counts") or {}).items():
        if names.count(tool) != times:
            return False, f"called {tool} {names.count(tool)} times, expected {times}"
    rest = iter(names)
    if not all(any(name == tool for name in rest) for tool in expect.get("call_sequence", [])):

    if absent:

    present = [text for text in expect.get("reply_not_contains", []) if text.lower() in low]
    if present:

import json, sys

content.thinking:
This is a per-key rate limit, and the reason field got truncated at 200 characters, showing a hashed key prefix rather than the actual key — it's a sha256-style hash identifier LiteLLM uses internally, not secret but still something I'd rather not spread unnecessarily given it's now sitting in this transcript. A truncated hash fragment isn't exploitable on its own, though I should note this reason also gets recorded in the case record.

I should scrub the hash prefix from any case record if it leaks through a VOID replay, and briefly flag this to the user rather than hiding it. On the rate limit itself, it looks like a per-minute requests/tokens cap on the gateway key, and with 3 parallel calls at ~5k tokens each we're blowing past TPM — the fix is dropping parallelism to 1 or 2 and lengthening the void retry waits, since the current 2s/8s backoff is too short for a per-minute limit. The simplest approach is probably adding an optional `void_waits` field to the case config so I can set something like 15s/45s instead of hardcoding an env var or CLI flag.

A VOID verdict in the lineup shouldn't count toward anything meaningful. My plan now is to add void_waits to Case, rerun the suite at parallelism 2 across all cases, then specifically redo the ones that failed under the bad reference.

# Real re-run summary (signature bisect, weighted bisect, single repeat, throttling)

Target support-agent-demo, good `1b40b27` (verified: 18/19 executed cases pass at it; es2 fails there too, ca/ms skipped because
cancel_order does not exist yet), bad `f7d82b7` (HEAD before the tracing/flaky commits; all three regressions present). DEMO_FLAKE=0,
AGENT_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5, JUDGE_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5 via the llm-proxy (concurrency 4, subscription backend), 1 repeat,
bad trace e2dad535... (rw1). Token baseline: merged calibration from 1b40b27 (3 repeats) plus ec19917 for the cancel_order cases
(`rerun2-baseline.json`). Without a baseline the harness skips token budgets, and R1/R2 are invisible (they only show as budget failures).

## Result per signature (run 2, after the fixes below)
| signature | culprit found | verdict | revert test |
|---|---|---|---|
| call_args:issue_refund.amount (R3, rw) | `b0be626` cents | CORRECT, confidence medium (revert conflicts flag) | passed 0% -> 100% |
| budget:tokens@refund_within_policy (rw) | `59c8b10` | plausible R2 (verify-with-search_help), confounded | failed 50% -> 50% |
| budget:tokens@order_status (os, R1 cases) | `59c8b10` | not a separate R1 culprit; same commit as above | failed 50% -> 0% |
| budget:tokens@policy_question (po, R2 cases) | `f7d82b7` | WRONG (borderline noise at the last commit) | failed 0% -> 50% |
| budget:tokens@escalation (es, R2 cases) | `ca150c7` | WRONG/unconfirmed | failed |
| budget:tokens@cancel_request (ca) | `96de44a` | unverified (revert inconclusive) | inconclusive |
| budget:tokens@multi_step (ms, R1 cases) | `22f7fbd` | unverified, 1 case, 1 sample | failed |
| call_args:escalate_to_human.priority (es2) | none | correctly refused: es2 fails at the good end too (not a regression) | n/a |

Success criteria: only R3 got its own culprit with a passing revert test. R1 and R2 were NOT separated: ground_truth.json only maps
cases to regressions (os/ms -> R1, po/es -> R2), not culprit commits, so the table scores case mapping and commit-message plausibility.
Every token regression inflates every category (the added tool schema and the search_help rule both lengthen every call), so
per-category budget signatures still mix R1 and R2 and the single-repeat token check is noisy near the 1.5x limit.

## Rounds
Primary (R3) investigation: 43 eval rounds including discovery. `compare` (separate empty caches): R3 plain 24 vs smart 21 rounds
(8 vs 7 steps), order_status budget plain 27 vs smart 24; same culprit both times. Smart wins by 3 rounds in both, but the
planner context was 21.7k tokens with the graph vs 43.3k reading the raw range (and 22.3k vs 39.4k). All 8 investigations: about 125
eval rounds plus compare reruns. Proxy totals for the whole session: 1417 calls (553 real CLI calls, 864 cache hits), 0 rate-limit
events, 0 backoff/recovered/gave_up events, 0 retries. No rate limiting was provoked at concurrency 4, so the live backoff path is
still only fake-tested.

## Bugs found and fixed (one commit each, 146 tests pass)
1. Budget regressions in different features collapsed into one `budget:tokens` signature; the suite only covered the bad trace's
   category (so R1/R2 cases never ran); one flaky rw3 run spawned three noise sibling investigations (call_args/must_call/call_counts).
   Fix: budget keys are `budget:tokens@<category>` (bare key still matches), `--all-categories`, signatures seen in a single run are
   re-run once and dropped if not reproduced (`signatures_unconfirmed`). Reviewer pass found three issues, all fixed.
2. A signature whose cases do not exist at the good end (cancel_order cases) made the good end "unusable". Now vacuously good.
   Resumed the two affected siblings; the other six ran on the code before this fix.
Run 1 (before fixes, `evidence/rerun1-prefix/`): R3 found at `b0be626`, budget at `59c8b10`, three noise siblings.

I'm thinking through whether GitHub Pages will correctly publish pages placed in a subfolder like `cases/outside/`, since relative links and the casebook's file globbing only look within a single folder—so I may need to keep the outside pages flat alongside the others instead.

Actually, simpler plan: have the casebook also collect records from subfolders, write their pages next to their records, and list them under a separate "Somebody else's repo" heading in the index. The tricky part is that subfolder pages would break the nav brand link and og image path since those are hardcoded to `index.html`, so I'm patching the rendered HTML after the fact to rewrite those hrefs to `../index.html` for subfolder pages—a bit hacky but contained. Writing the subfolder iteration logic...

I'm also adding a `more` parameter to the index renderer so extra sections of records can be shown under custom headings, with a simple constant mapping like `{"outside": ("Outside cases", description)}` rather than trying to auto-generate headings from README files. Now I'm wondering what the case page actually renders for these "outside" records that only have lineup and motive but no evidence/brief/fix/damages—there should be a state for planted records like this, and the headline copy ("25 commits since it last worked...") should still work fine. The remaining concern is whether the Entire checkpoint link will even resolve, since it's built from the repo's git remote and points to entire.io's mirror of that repo—if the demo repo isn't actually mirrored there, that link could 404.

I need to check how `case.repo` is resolved relative to cwd versus the actual repo directory, since right now it looks like it could fall back to the wrong repo path and point the link to the wrong project entirely. For the docket totals, I'm planning to keep the main six cases on their own summary line and give the outside group its own separate line, computing replay cost from token counts using the haiku pricing table since damages data is absent for these. I still need to figure out what stamp text to use for these records—something like "Culprit named" or "Range clear"—so I should check the stamp function and how it's tested.

Scoring confirms one accusation matches the key while the other doesn't, and the two token-cost regressions fall outside what these checks can verify. Next, I'll generate the outside case pages and the write-up.

content.thinking:
The page looks fine overall, though some edge cases feel rough, like the "Read the brief" button showing when there's no brief, or sections saying "No brief yet" or "Not fixed yet." Since the instruction was not to run a fix for outside cases, I think it's fine for those sections to plainly state that nothing was asked for, maybe adding a small note field on the case record explaining it's from someone else's repo and only the commit was named.

I'm also wondering whether the page should flag that the repo's own answer key doesn't actually list this breakage under this commit — the user's instruction about saying so "if it does" was specifically about motive fallback, which didn't happen here, so this is a different honesty concern. I don't see an existing notes slot for this in the schema, and adding a new "scored" key to the record feels like it would require a separate scripted step I'm not sure is in scope, so I'm leaning toward leaving this alone unless the sealed eval pages show similar scoring elsewhere, which they don't seem to.

The third case fails at both ends, 6 of 6 and 6 of 6, so the lineup named nobody and said no commit in the range did it. The motive step worked on their repo, which I had not expected. Their checkpoint branch is published, so the request behind `b0be626` came out of its Entire checkpoint, was found word for word in the session transcript, and `entire why` put all 12 changed lines that were checked behind that commit and checkpoint. The request asked for refund amounts in cents "to match Stripe", with the change kept to the refund tool and its tests. ## What the key says [ground_truth.json](https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/agentbisect/blob/main/evidence/ground_truth.json) maps each of their 24 eval cases to one of three seeded regressions, R1, R2 and R3, or to "control". It names no commits. Their notes beside it (`evidence/rerun-summary.md` and `evidence/rerun3-summary.md`) say what the three are: R3 is the refund amount in cents, at `b0be626`. R1 and R2 are changes that make every run use more tokens, one through a tool schema and one through a rule about `search_help`, and their notes point at `59c8b10` for R2 and name no commit for R1. The key puts es2 under R2, the token regression, and Whodunit named R3's commit. What the replays show is a different symptom from the one the key means. Before `b0be626` the agent sent an 800.00 refund request to a person every time, and from that commit on it issued the refund itself every time. That commit reworded the tool's own rule that refunds over $500 must be escalated. So this may be a side effect of R3 that the key does not list, or it may be something only the model on this gateway does. Nobody has reverted the commit to find out, and I am not counting it as a hit. - out-of-window: agrees with the key. ro1 is a control, and Whodunit named nobody. - R1 and R2: not found, and not looked for. Every request their key files under R1 or R2 still called the right tools and said the right things at the bad ref, twice each, except es1, which fails the same way at both ends. A check on tools and replies cannot see a run that is right and costs more. The token counts were there to see: the same order-status request used 4,562 input tokens at the bad ref and a refund request that used 2,904 at the good ref used 4,576 at the bad one. No case was opened on them, because the cases were to come from the repo's own checks. So, plainly: of three seeded regressions, Whodunit named the commit behind one. It made two accusations, one confirmed by the key and one the key does not back. It called one range clear, correctly. Their notes also record a behaviour at the tip commit, cancelling an unshipped order when the customer only asked where it was, which their tool caught. All five of their order-status requests passed 2 times in 2 here at the tip, so no case was opened for it. ## What it cost All of it ran on the hackathon gateway's small model, two replays at a time, with token counts taken from what the agent prints and priced at $1 and $5 per million. - Screening their 24 eval inputs at the bad ref twice, and the ones that failed at the good ref twice: 67 runs, 359,913 input tokens and 13,379 output tokens, about $0.43. - The three lineups: 56 replays, about $0.41. - About $0.83 in all, against a cap of $2.50 the owner set. ## What had to change in Whodunit - A check that is not about refunds. `kind = "calls"` reads the JSON an agent prints and checks which tools it called, which it did not, the first call, counts, order, arguments, and what the reply says or matches. The case says where in the JSON the calls and the reply are. An expectation it does not know is refused, so a misspelt one cannot pass by being ignored. - Reading a result that is pretty-printed over many lines. The refund agent prints one line. - Handing an agent its key under the agent's own name. `[env_from]` in a case maps the agent's variable to the name of one in the runner's `.env`. Only names are written down. - A longer wait after a provider error, set per case, because this gateway limits by the minute and the first screening run lost 15 attempts to that at three at a time. - Token counts on each replay, when the agent reports them. - A record keeps the address of the repo it was run on, so the page links the culprit's own Entire page. No file in their repo was edited. The gateway was reached through environment variables alone. ## What did not carry over - Alibis. The agent sits at the root of its repo, so the path filter excuses nobody, and entire-graph was not set up in the clone. All 25 commits started equal. A README-only commit was as suspect as the rest. - Traces. The agent's own tracing was switched off for these replays so that its runs went to nobody's neatlogs project. So there is no failing run set against a passing one, and no brief. - Damages. Those are still read from the refund agent's tool spans. - The fix. It was not run, on purpose. Their repo is theirs to fix. - The model. Their notes say they ran the agent on its pinned model through their own proxy. These replays used the gateway's small model, which may not be the same version. Two of their cases that they report passing at the good ref fail there here, and their es2 fails at the good ref in both places. ## What was not checked - Whether the skipped escalation really starts at `b0be626` on their pinned model. That needs their setup, or a revert, and neither was done. - Whether a token check would have found R1 and R2. It was not built. - The lineups were run once each. At temperature 0 the agent is close to deterministic, which is why 22 replays were enough, and why these two cases say little about the statistical part of the bisect. ### $NOW, Monday: one history somebody else wrote

The second finding from the owner's review: everything was measured on a refund agent whose history was grown here. This is one run on a repo that was not, https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/support-agent-demo by Jaxson Sprinkles, the target another neatHack team built for their own tool. The owner approved a clone of it outside this repo. \`eval/outside/README.md\` has the whole account, and this is the short one.

What was done:

- A new check, \`kind = "calls"\`, judges a run by the tools it called and what it replied, read from the JSON it prints. With it came four smaller things a foreign agent needed: reading pretty-printed JSON, \`env_from\` to hand over a key by name, \`void_waits\` for a gateway that limits by the minute, and token counts on each replay.
- Their agent ran on the hackathon gateway through environment variables alone. No file of theirs was edited.
- I ran their 24 eval inputs at the bad ref and the failing ones at the good ref, and wrote three cases from the ones that told the ends apart or plainly did not.
- Two lineups each named \`b0be626\` at 97.9% after 22 replays across 7 of 25 commits. The third found the request failing 6 of 6 at both ends and named nobody.
- The motive step found the request behind \`b0be626\` in their Entire checkpoint and checked the quote against the transcript. The owner and I had both expected it to fall back to the commit message, because their checkpoint branch did not look published. It is.
- \`eval/outside/predictions.json\` was committed and pushed in \`d1bf1b0\` at 5:19 PM. Only then did I clone their other repo and read the key.

How it scored:

- Their key seeds three regressions. One is the refund amount in cents, at \`b0be626\`. Whodunit named it. That is the hit.
- The other two make every run use more tokens and leave its answers right. A check on tools and replies cannot see that, so Whodunit did not find them and had no case that could have.
- The second accusation is not backed by the key. The key files that request under one of the token regressions. Whodunit named \`b0be626\` for it, on a different symptom: the agent refunding an 800.00 order itself where it had been sending it to a person, 10 of 10 replays from that commit on against 12 of 12 before. It may be a side effect their key does not list, or something only this gateway's model does. It is written up as not backed, and not as a hit.
- The clear range agrees with the key, which lists that request as a control.

What went wrong:

- The first screening run, three at a time, hit the gateway's per-minute limit and lost 15 attempts. All were voided and run again, and two requests ended void. From then on replays ran two at a time with waits of 20 and 45 seconds.
- A voided replay's reason quotes the gateway's error, and that error carries the first characters of a hash of the key. One such line was printed in this session. It is not the key and cannot be used as one. No record under \`cases/outside/\` holds it.
- My first test for the argument matcher put two conditions in one table and the matcher allowed one. It now takes several and all must hold.
- The write-up first gave a token comparison I had not measured for the same request at both ends. It now quotes the one pair I did measure.

Spend, from the token counts the agent prints, at \$1 and \$5 per million: 67 screening runs for about \$0.43 and 56 lineup replays for about \$0.41. About \$0.83 of the \$2.50 the owner allowed, all on the gateway. The owner's own key was not used.

Checked: 156 fast tests pass, 6 of them new. The casebook lists the three cases under a heading of their own, and each page links back to it and says how its answer scored.

Not checked: whether the skipped escalation starts at \`b0be626\` on their own pinned model, since nothing was reverted and their setup was not used. Whether a token check would find the other two. The lineups were run once each, and at temperature 0 they say little about the statistical part of the bisect. The casebook headline takes four lines at phone width, one more than the design rule allows, and I left it.

# Write a neatroots check

1. Restate the failure as a yes/no question phrased as a failure ("Did the agent … without …?"), so
   that yes means a problem. Decide whether one span shows it (`scope: span`) or it needs the run
   (`scope: trace`).

   YAML yourself (see `docs/checks.md`). Prefer a **rule** when the failure is mechanical (same call
   repeated, an error streak, a regex on output): rules are exact and free.
3. Preview: `preview_check` with the draft. A good check fires on the runs that have the bug and few
   others. If it fires everywhere, make the question more specific; if nowhere, check the evidence
   selector (span types and names).

   `~/.neatroots/checks`) or `dir` set to the repo's `.neatroots/checks` so the team gets it too.

content.content:
4. questions the planner or a coding agent wrote (kept in the database until you save them).

## Rules

Code, no model, every span.

```yaml
id: repeated-tool-call
kind: rule
title: Same tool called repeatedly with identical arguments
rule:
  type: repeat            # repeat | errors | count | threshold | match | run_end
  span: { type: [tool, mcp_tool] }
  same: [tool, input]
  at_least: 3
guidance: >-
  You have called {tool} {count} times with the same arguments ({args}) ...
action: flag              # or halt (your own rules only)
```

| type | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `repeat` | `at_least` matching spans share the `same` fields; resolves when the next call differs |
| `errors` | `consecutive` matching spans failed in a row |
| `count` | the run has `at_least` matching spans |
| `threshold` | a run metric (`total_tokens`, `llm_calls`, `duration_ms`, …) reaches `at_least` |
| `match` | a regex matches a span's `input`, `output`, `error` or `name` |
| `run_end` | the run ended with `error`, `no_output` or `interrupted` |

## Questions

Answered by the decision model with a probability. Yes/no questions are phrased as failures, so a
high probability always means a problem.

```yaml
id: refund-without-ownership
kind: yes_no              # yes_no | choice | score
scope: trace              # span | trace | session
ask: Did the agent issue a refund without first confirming the customer owns the order?
evidence:
  spans: { type: tool, name: [lookup_order, issue_refund] }
  fields: [input, output, status]
  last: 12
  final_output: false
when: live                # live (as spans arrive, and at run end) | end
flag_at: 0.8
guidance: Confirm the customer owns the order before issuing a refund.
applies_to: { workflow: refund-agent }
```

`choice` questions take `options` (label → description) and `flag_on`; `score` questions take
`levels` and `flag_at_level`.

### Make sure a question can see what it asks about

- `scope: span` judges one call at a time: right for "Did this tool call pass a negative amount?".
- `scope: trace` sees the run's spans in order: right whenever a question relates two things, such
  as a tool's result and what the agent said next.
- A question about the agent's answer ("claims", "says", "reports", "the final response") needs
  `scope: trace` and `evidence.final_output: true`. `neatroots checks validate`, the app's check
  editor and the MCP check tools warn when a check asks about the answer but can't see it; a check
  drafted from a plain-language concern is given that evidence automatically.
- Preview a new check on at least one run that has the problem and one that doesn't.

The rules can't directly express "A without earlier B" since they only support counting matching spans, not absence. There's a yes_no example in the docs involving refund-without-ownership that would require the local qwen2.5:3b model, but running it across up to 200 preview runs would be slow and load the machine.

"""Count the recorded refund-agent runs that issued a refund with no lookup before it, by where their commit sits.

This is the headline case turned into something to watch for: `issue_refund` called in a run where no
`lookup_order` came first. It reads neatroots, uses no model, and prints one JSON object.

    uv run python eval/standing_check.py
"""

import json
import subprocess
from collections import Counter

from whodunit.neat import neatroots, select_all

CULPRIT = "ced2ecd21c3ed165a1a729e17f68d2000cdc19ca"  # cases/whole-history.record.json, lineup.culprit
FIX = "7e8120e7a5bd05c5d54b542b8a2794fdbd6fc229"  # the same record, fix.commit


def holds(ancestor: str, sha: str) -> bool:
    return subprocess.run(["git", "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", ancestor, sha], capture_output=True).returncode == 0


def main() -> None:
    mcp = neatroots()
    runs = select_all(mcp, "select r.trace_id, s.attributes from runs r join spans s on s.trace_id = r.trace_id and s.name = 'run_info' "
                           "where r.workflow = 'refund-agent' and r.complete = 1", cap=20000)
    flagged = {row["trace_id"] for row in select_all(
        mcp, "select distinct f.trace_id from spans f where f.name = 'issue_refund' and not exists "
             "(select 1 from spans l where l.trace_id = f.trace_id and l.name = 'lookup_order' and l.start_ms < f.start_ms)", cap=20000)}
    where: dict[str, str] = {}
    seen, hits = Counter(), Counter()
    for row in runs:
        tags = json.loads(row["attributes"]).get("neatlogs.tags") or json.loads(row["attributes"]).get("tags") or row["attributes"]
        text = tags if isinstance(tags, str) else json.dumps(tags)
        at = text.find("commit:")
        sha = "".join(ch for ch in text[at + 7:at + 47] if ch in "0123456789abcdef") if at >= 0 else ""
        if len(sha) < 7:
            place = "no commit tag"
        else:
            if sha not in where:
                known = subprocess.run(["git", "cat-file", "-e", f"{sha}^{{commit}}"], capture_output=True).returncode == 0
                where[sha] = ("commit not in this repo" if not known else "at the kept fix" if holds(FIX, sha)
                              else "from the culprit on, unfixed" if holds(CULPRIT, sha) else "before the culprit")
            place = where[sha]
        seen[place] += 1
        hits[place] += row["trace_id"] in flagged
    print(json.dumps({"runs": sum(seen.values()), "flagged": sum(hits.values()),
                      "by_place": {place: {"runs": seen[place], "flagged": hits[place]} for place in sorted(seen)}}, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF

# Business plan inputs

These are the numbers and assumptions to build the cfo.ai model from. The measured ones come from this repo's runs on 10 and 11 October 2026. The assumed ones are marked and are the owner's to change.

One thing to keep in view when quoting any of it: no real customer has used the refund agent. Its ordinary traffic was sent by `eval/traffic.py`, a script that plays customers against each commit, and the shop and its orders are test data. The replay costs below are real spend on real model calls. The refund amounts are what a script's requests cost a test shop.

## What is being sold

Whodunit Cloud: hosted investigations for teams that run an AI agent in production. The command line tool stays open source and free with your own keys. The paid product is the hosted replay workers, the case file pages, the regression checks in CI, and the standing rulings shared across a team.

## Unit costs, measured

Six full investigations on the refund agent, with replays on a small hosted model at list price:

| Case | Replays | Replay cost |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| cents-off | 89 | $0.34 |
| strangers-paid | 112 | $0.39 |
| whole-history | 176 | $0.80 |
| turned-away | 171 | $0.95 |
| wrong-order-refunded | 274 | $1.00 |
| half-done-batch | 558 | $3.53 |

- Median replay cost per investigation: about $0.87. Mean: about $1.17. The worst case is a rare bug that was never fixed. These are higher than the first version of this table, because every kept fix is now also replayed against 12 or 13 other requests, and the headline case needed a second patch.
- Brief and patch calls on a larger model: about $0.10 to $0.30 per investigation.
- Replay worker: one t3.large at about $61 a month runs three replays at a time. Assumed: one worker per 15 paying teams.
- So the cost of one investigation is about $1.37 on average for an agent on a small model. An agent on a large model costs roughly 5 to 15 times more to replay, which is why replays are billed at cost above the included amount.

## What a regression costs the customer, counted from scripted traffic

The requests were sent by `eval/traffic.py`, not by customers, so these show the size of the thing and are not a measurement of any real shop. Each line counts only the runs that failed that case's own check:

- One prompt change refunded 120.00 to the wrong people, in 4 of the 6 scripted requests that asked for it.
- One "friendlier replies" change withheld 360.00, across all 6 scripted requests that were owed a refund: three of 90.00 and three of 30.00.
- These come from a few hundred scripted requests spread over the history. A real shop would see them at its own volume until someone noticed.

## Pricing, assumed

| Plan | Price | Included |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Open source | $0 | The CLI, your own keys, your own machine |
| Team | $249 a month per agent | 40 investigations, hosted replays on a small model, CI regression checks |
| Scale | $999 a month per agent | 250 investigations, private replay worker, single sign-on |
| Extra investigations | $8 each | |
| Replays on the customer's larger model | at cost plus 20% | |

Gross margin on Team at full use: 40 investigations at $1.37 is $55, plus about $4 of worker share, against $249. About 76%.

## Costs, assumed

| Item | Monthly |
| --- | ---: |
| Founder draw, months 1 to 6 | $0 |
| Founder draw, month 7 on | $3,000 |
| Replay workers and hosting | $150, plus $61 per 15 teams |
| Model spend for development and evals | $300 |
| Tools (tracing, checkpoints, finance) | $150 |
| Legal and accounting | $100 |
